link.title: Beyond ‘It Looks Good’: A Production RAG Evaluation Framework

entry.content:
RAG Evaluation LLM-as-Judge RAGAS AWS Bedrock

Beyond "It Looks Good": A Production RAG Evaluation Framework

If you can't measure the quality of your RAG system, you can't confidently improve it. This guide covers how to build a production-grade evaluation framework — comparing open-source (RAGAS) with managed (Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations), with architecture patterns for offline, online, and CI/CD-integrated pipelines.

On this page
Why RAG Evaluation? Evaluation Lifecycle Evaluation as a Pipeline Metrics Taxonomy Quantitative vs Qualitative Architecture Patterns RAGAS Deep Dive AgentCore Evaluations Framework Comparison CI/CD Integration Custom Rubrics Maturity Model

Why RAG Evaluation Matters

Teams spend weeks experimenting with embedding models, chunking strategies, rerankers, prompts, and LLMs. A change may feel like an improvement because it produces a few impressive examples — but without structured evaluation, there is no objective way to answer:

Question
Did retrieval actually improve?
Changing the embedding model or chunk size might help some queries and hurt others. Without metrics, you'll never know the net effect.
Question
Did hallucinations decrease?
A model upgrade that sounds more fluent might actually hallucinate more. Faithfulness metrics catch this before users do.
Question
Is the newer model worth the cost?
A 3x more expensive LLM that only improves answer quality by 2% might not justify the spend. Evaluation quantifies the tradeoff.
The Real Problem

RAG systems have multiple moving parts — ingestion, chunking, embedding, retrieval, reranking, prompting, and generation. If the final answer is wrong, the problem could be at any stage. Without evaluating each stage independently, debugging becomes guesswork.

The Evaluation Lifecycle

Evaluation is not a one-time activity — it's a continuous cycle that begins before the system is even deployed. The lifecycle starts with synthetic test set generation and loops back through human review at every stage.

  • 1. Synthetic Test Set Generation
    LLMs automatically generate evaluation questions, expected answers, and relevant contexts from your enterprise documents. This creates a representative benchmark dataset without months of manual curation. Tools like RAGAS TestsetGenerator or custom prompting pipelines produce diverse question types — factual, multi-hop, reasoning, comparison — covering the breadth of real user queries.
  • 2. Human Review & Curation
    Domain experts review the synthetic test set — validating questions for relevance, correcting expected answers, removing duplicates, and adding edge cases that synthetic generation missed. This human-in-the-loop step transforms a rough synthetic set into a golden benchmark dataset that reflects real-world complexity.
  • 3. Run Evaluation Against the Agent
    Execute the curated test set against the RAG system. Collect traces (question → retrieved context → generated answer) and compute metrics across retrieval and generation stages. This establishes the performance baseline.
  • 4. Iterate on Configuration Changes
    Whenever the agent configuration changes — new embedding model, updated chunking strategy, prompt modification, LLM upgrade, reranker tuning — re-run the evaluation against the same golden dataset. This ensures every change is measured, not assumed to be an improvement.
  • 5. Compare Results Against Baseline
    Generate per-question verdicts (PASS / IMPROVE / FAIL) by comparing candidate scores against the baseline. Use weighted metric thresholds to determine whether the change is a net positive. Identify regressions early — before they reach production.
  • 6. Human Review of Results & Feedback Loop
    Stakeholders and domain experts review evaluation results — especially low-scoring questions and borderline verdicts. Their feedback feeds back into the cycle: updating the test set with new edge cases, refining expected answers, adjusting metric weights, or identifying areas where the rubric itself needs improvement.
Why Start with Synthetic Generation?

Creating evaluation datasets manually is expensive and slow — typically taking weeks for a team to produce a few hundred questions. Synthetic generation produces thousands of diverse questions in hours, covering corner cases humans wouldn't think to test. The human review step then ensures quality without the bottleneck of manual creation from scratch.

The Feedback Loop is Critical

Step 6 is what separates mature evaluation from a one-shot benchmark. Human feedback refines the test set over time — adding questions that exposed real production failures, removing outdated questions after system changes, and continuously raising the quality bar. The golden dataset evolves with the system.

Evaluation as a Pipeline

Rather than evaluating only the final answer, production systems evaluate multiple stages independently. This separation identifies exactly where quality is lost.

  • Stage 1: Retrieval Evaluation
    Did the system retrieve the right information? Measures whether relevant documents make it into the context window.
  • Stage 2: Generation Evaluation
    Did the LLM use the retrieved context correctly? Checks faithfulness, relevance, and completeness of the generated answer.
  • Stage 3: End-to-End Evaluation
    Does the overall system meet user expectations? Measures task success, latency, cost, safety, and user satisfaction.
Key Insight

A system can have perfect retrieval but poor generation (LLM ignores context), or perfect generation but poor retrieval (right answer for the wrong reasons). Evaluating stages independently reveals which component to optimize.

Metrics Taxonomy

Retrieval Metrics

MetricWhat It MeasuresWhy It Matters
Context PrecisionHow much retrieved context is relevantLess noise reaching the LLM = fewer hallucinations
Context RecallDid retrieval find all important informationMissing context = incomplete answers
Hit Rate (Hit@K)Was the correct doc in top K resultsBaseline retrieval effectiveness
MRRHow highly the correct doc appearsHigher rank = better LLM attention
NDCGRanking quality with graded relevanceRewards placing best docs at the top

Generation Metrics

MetricWhat It MeasuresWhy It Matters
FaithfulnessIs every claim supported by contextDirectly measures hallucination — the #1 stakeholder concern
Answer RelevanceDoes the answer address the questionCatches technically correct but off-topic responses
CompletenessDoes the answer cover all aspectsPartial answers frustrate users
CorrectnessHow close to a reference answerGround-truth comparison when available
Context UtilizationDid the model use the retrieved contextExcellent context retrieved but ignored = wasted retrieval

End-to-End Metrics

Task
Success Rate
Latency
Response Time
Cost
Per Query
Hallucination
Rate
Safety
Compliance

Quantitative vs Qualitative Evaluation

Statistical
Quantitative Metrics
Objective numerical scores: Precision, Recall, Hit Rate, MRR, NDCG, ROUGE, BLEU, METEOR. Repeatable, easy to compare over time, integrated into dashboards. But can't capture nuance.
LLM-as-Judge
Qualitative Metrics
An LLM evaluates outputs against criteria: helpfulness, faithfulness, clarity, groundedness, completeness. Scales better than human review while capturing nuances statistical metrics miss.

The most effective evaluation strategies combine both — statistical metrics for regression detection and automated benchmarking, LLM-as-Judge for quality dimensions that require reasoning.

Architecture: Offline, Online, and Hybrid

A production evaluation system operates across three modes:

Pre-Deploy
Offline (Batch) Evaluation
Run against curated benchmark datasets before deployment. Compare candidate vs baseline using golden datasets. Gate deployments on metric thresholds. Regression testing for every change.
Post-Deploy
Online (Live) Evaluation
Continuously monitor production traffic. Sample a percentage of sessions (e.g., 10%). Track quality trends over time. Alert on degradation. No golden dataset needed — evaluates against rubrics.
On-Demand
Targeted Investigation
Evaluate specific sessions or traces. Investigate reported issues. Validate fixes. Analyze historical data. Useful for debugging and root-cause analysis of quality problems.

Evaluation Pipeline Architecture

  • Ingest
    Collect agent traces (question, retrieved context, generated answer, tool calls) — via OpenTelemetry, application logs, or direct API capture.
  • Enqueue
    Queue evaluation jobs (SQS, Kafka, or managed service). Decouple evaluation from the serving path to avoid latency impact.
  • Evaluate
    Workers execute metric computations — statistical metrics in parallel with LLM-as-Judge scoring. Multiple evaluators run concurrently per trace.
  • Store
    Persist scores with full lineage (trace ID, evaluator version, model used). Enables historical trending and A/B comparison.
  • Verdict
    Compare against baselines — generate PASS/IMPROVE/FAIL verdicts per question using configurable thresholds and weighted metrics.
  • Report
    Dashboard visualization, CloudWatch metrics for alerting, natural-language summaries for stakeholders, and CI/CD gate decisions.

RAGAS: Open-Source Evaluation

RAGAS (Retrieval Augmented Generation Assessment) is the most widely adopted open-source framework for RAG evaluation. It provides both retrieval and generation metrics, all computed using LLM-as-Judge under the hood.

Core Metrics

MetricCategoryWhat It Evaluates
FaithfulnessGenerationClaims in the answer supported by retrieved context
Answer RelevancyGenerationWhether the answer addresses the question asked
Answer CorrectnessGenerationSemantic similarity to a reference answer
Answer SimilarityGenerationSurface-level similarity to reference
Context PrecisionRetrievalProportion of retrieved context that is relevant
Context RecallRetrievalProportion of relevant information retrieved
Context Entity RecallRetrievalNamed entities from ground truth found in context
Context UtilizationGenerationHow effectively the model uses retrieved context

Agentic Evaluation Metrics

For multi-turn agent interactions, RAGAS provides:

Agent
Agent Goal Accuracy
Did the agent achieve the user's stated goal across the full multi-turn interaction? Evaluates end-to-end task completion.
Agent
Tool Call Accuracy
Did the agent invoke the correct tools with the right parameters? Measures whether the agent's reasoning led to appropriate tool selection.
RAGAS Strengths

No vendor lock-in. Fully extensible. Works with any LLM provider. Integrates into CI/CD pipelines. Active open-source community. Supports custom metrics. Reference-free evaluation possible (no golden dataset required for some metrics).

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations

AgentCore Evaluations is AWS's managed evaluation service. It uses LLM-as-Judge techniques with both built-in and custom evaluators, integrating with OpenTelemetry and OpenInference instrumentation.

Evaluation Types

Continuous
Online Evaluation
Monitors live production traffic continuously. Configurable sampling (e.g., 10% of sessions). Conditional filters for targeted evaluation. Aggregated dashboards with trend tracking.
Targeted
On-Demand Evaluation
Evaluate specific spans or traces by ID. Investigate customer interactions. Validate fixes. Analyze historical data. Ideal for build-time testing and issue investigation.
Bulk
Batch Evaluation
Process multiple sessions in a single async job. Supports ground truth via session metadata. Pre/post comparison for prompt or model updates. Regression testing across curated sets.

Built-in Evaluators

AgentCore provides pre-configured evaluators accessible via ARN (e.g., Builtin.Helpfulness). These use optimized prompt templates and cannot be modified — ensuring consistent scoring baselines.

Custom Evaluators

Define domain-specific evaluation criteria with custom prompt templates and evaluator models. Custom evaluators are private resources with IAM-based access control — enabling team-specific quality criteria without exposing evaluation logic.

AgentCore Strengths

Fully managed — no infrastructure to maintain. Native integration with Strands and LangGraph agents. OpenTelemetry trace ingestion. Session sampling and filtering. Aggregate dashboards built-in. Supports up to 1M input/output tokens per minute per account.

Framework Comparison: RAGAS vs AgentCore Evaluations

DimensionRAGAS (Open Source)Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
DeploymentSelf-hosted (your infra)Fully managed (AWS)
LLM ProviderAny (OpenAI, Bedrock, local)Bedrock models
Retrieval Metrics✓ Context Precision, Recall, Entity Recall~ Via custom evaluators
Generation Metrics✓ Faithfulness, Relevancy, Correctness✓ Helpfulness, Correctness (built-in)
Agentic Metrics✓ Goal Accuracy, Tool Call Accuracy✓ Goal attainment, tool accuracy
NLP Metrics~ Via integration✗ Not built-in
Online Evaluation~ Build your own pipeline✓ Native with sampling + filters
Batch Evaluation✓ With custom orchestration✓ Managed async jobs
Custom Rubrics✓ Fully extensible✓ Custom evaluators with IAM
CI/CD Integration✓ Native (Python, any CI)✓ Via SDK/CLI
Ground Truth Support✓ Reference-based + reference-free✓ Via session metadata
Dashboards✗ Build your own✓ Built-in aggregation
Trace Integration~ Manual✓ OpenTelemetry native
Vendor Lock-in✓ None✗ AWS
CostLLM inference costs onlyLLM inference + service fees
Best ForTeams needing full control, multi-cloudTeams on AWS wanting managed ops

CI/CD Integration: Evaluate Before You Ship

Every change to a RAG system — embedding model, chunk size, retriever, reranker, prompt, LLM — should be validated against evaluation benchmarks before deployment.

CI/CD Evaluation Pipeline

  • Trigger
    PR or commit triggers evaluation workflow (GitHub Actions, Jenkins, or any CI).
  • Run Candidate
    Execute the changed RAG system against the golden evaluation dataset. Collect traces (question, context, answer).
  • Evaluate
    Run RAGAS metrics (or AgentCore batch evaluation) on collected traces. Compute all configured metrics.
  • Compare
    Compare candidate scores against the baseline. Generate per-question verdicts (PASS / IMPROVE / FAIL) with configurable thresholds.
  • Gate
    Block deployment if weighted metric score drops below threshold. Report results as PR comments or CI annotations.
  • Promote
    On pass, the candidate becomes the new baseline. Store results for historical tracking.
A/B Testing in Practice

Instead of relying on intuition, run A/B tests against the same evaluation dataset. Compare retrieval metrics, generation metrics, latency, and cost. Only promote changes that demonstrate measurable improvements across the metric set.

Custom Domain-Specific Rubrics

Generic metrics are rarely sufficient in enterprise environments. A technically correct answer may still fail because it omitted required information, violated policies, or missed domain-specific criteria.

Domain
Regulatory Compliance
Does the answer comply with industry regulations? Are required disclaimers present? Are citations to approved sources included?
Domain
Citation Completeness
Are all factual claims traced to a source? Are references valid and verifiable? Does the citation format match organizational standards?
Domain
Business Rule Validation
Does the answer respect business constraints? Are deprecated configurations flagged? Are prerequisite conditions mentioned?
Domain
Knowledge Coverage
Does the answer utilize all relevant internal knowledge? Are cross-references to related topics included? Is context from multiple sources synthesized?

Both RAGAS and AgentCore support custom rubrics — RAGAS through extensible Python classes, AgentCore through custom evaluator resources with configurable prompt templates.

Evaluation Maturity Model

Teams don't need to build everything at once. A practical path to production-grade evaluation:

  • Level 1: Manual Spot-Checks
    Human reviewers sample outputs periodically. No automation. High cost, low coverage. Where most teams start.
  • Level 2: Offline Benchmarks
    Golden dataset + automated RAGAS metrics in a notebook. Run before major changes. First measurable quality baseline.
  • Level 3: CI/CD-Gated Evaluation
    Every PR runs evaluation automatically. Deployment blocked on metric regression. Verdict system compares candidate vs baseline.
  • Level 4: Online Monitoring
    Live traffic evaluated continuously. Dashboards track trends. Alerts on quality degradation. Sampling-based to control cost.
  • Level 5: Continuous Optimization
    Evaluation drives automated A/B testing. System self-optimizes (prompt tuning, retrieval strategy selection) based on metric feedback loops.
The Bottom Line

The most successful teams treat evaluation as a first-class component of their architecture — just as important as retrieval, prompting, or model selection. A mature framework combines statistical metrics for objectivity, LLM-as-Judge for nuance, custom rubrics for domain relevance, and continuous monitoring for production safety.
entry.summary: A practical guide to building production-grade RAG evaluation — comparing RAGAS and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations, with architecture patterns for offline, online, and CI/CD-integrated evaluation pipelines.

entry.title: Knowledge Fabric: AI-Powered Technical Intelligence
entry.content:
Knowledge Graph RAG AI Agent Architecture

Knowledge Fabric: AI-Powered Technical Intelligence

A multi-layer architecture that transforms scattered technical documentation into an AI-queryable intelligence layer — connecting entities, parameters, dependencies, and metrics into a unified, traversable graph that an AI agent can reason over in a single round.

Architecture Pattern Multi-Layer Retrieval Entity-First Design Citation-Mandatory
On this page
The Problem What is a Knowledge Fabric? Architecture Query Traversal Why Not Standard RAG? Data Ingestion The AI Agent Access Patterns Design Principles Performance

The Problem: Documentation at Scale

Enterprise technical documentation is vast, distributed, and interconnected in ways no single search tool can navigate. Engineers face thousands of documents across dozens of formats — feature descriptions, configuration guides, parameter references, deployment procedures, impact reports, and performance metrics — each maintained by different teams, versioned independently, and cross-referencing each other implicitly.

The Real Cost

Traditional approaches — keyword search, manual cross-referencing, tribal knowledge — fail silently. Engineers get answers that are incomplete, outdated, or disconnected from the relationships that determine whether a configuration is safe to deploy.

Fragmented Information
Critical knowledge spans hundreds of documents. A single configuration decision may require cross-referencing feature descriptions, parameter guides, dependency trees, and deployment procedures.
Hidden Dependencies
Conflicts between features are buried in prose. Prerequisites are implicit. Impact chains traverse multiple document types. No single view connects them.
Version Drift
Documentation evolves across releases. Parameters change defaults, features get deprecated, new dependencies emerge. Keeping track manually doesn't scale.

What is a Knowledge Fabric?

A Knowledge Fabric is not a single database or a simple RAG pipeline. It is a multi-layer intelligence architecture where each layer specializes in a different type of retrieval — and an AI agent dynamically selects which layers to activate based on what the question requires.

The key insight: different questions need different retrieval strategies. A question about parameter values needs structured lookup. A question about dependencies needs graph traversal. A question about "how to deploy X" needs semantic search over procedural documentation. The Knowledge Fabric provides all of these through a unified interface.

Core Principle: Entity-First Resolution

Every query begins by resolving "what is this?" — determining the entity type (feature, parameter, metric, configuration class) before deciding "what about it?" This sub-100ms resolution step determines which layers are relevant, eliminating brute-force scanning across the entire corpus.

Architecture: Seven Interconnected Layers

The fabric is composed of specialized layers, each optimized for a different retrieval pattern. The layers are not isolated — they share entity identifiers, enabling cross-layer traversal in a single agent round.

1
Lexical
Entity Registry — name-to-type resolution. Acronym expansion. First hop for every query: determines routing to the correct downstream layer. Sub-100ms lookup.
2
Semantic
Vector embeddings with hybrid retrieval (kNN + BM25 + Reciprocal Rank Fusion). Entity-enriched metadata per chunk. Source-weighted boosting for high-value document types.
3
Relational
Knowledge graph of entities and their relationships — dependencies, conflicts, constraints, parameter sharing. Supports BFS traversal, topological sort, transitive impact analysis, and activation ordering.
4
Hierarchical
Parent-child containment trees for configuration objects. Maps which metrics belong to which configuration classes, with full attribute metadata (defaults, ranges, enumerations).
5
Structured
Typed fact tables — parameters, metrics, configuration steps, prerequisites, recommendations per deployment scenario. Precise point lookups with no ambiguity.
6
Temporal
Version evolution tracking — what was introduced, modified, or removed across releases. Enables release diff, deprecation tracking, and historical context for configuration decisions.
7
Bridge
Cross-domain index connecting entities across layers. Enables multi-hop queries: Feature → Configuration Class → Metrics, or Feature → Recommendation → Deployment Scenario.
Layer Interconnection

Every entity lives in multiple layers with shared identifiers. The Lexical layer resolves the entity and routes to the correct layer. The Bridge layer connects entities across domain boundaries. The Semantic layer fills gaps where structured data doesn't exist. No layer works in isolation.

How a Question Traverses the Fabric

When a user asks a question, the AI agent doesn't search all layers. It uses entity resolution to determine which layers are relevant, then executes tool calls in parallel — all in a single round. Click a question below to see which layers activate:

Select a query path:
Click a question to see the traversal path through the fabric layers.

Why Not Standard RAG?

Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation retrieves text chunks based on semantic similarity and passes them to an LLM. This works for simple questions but fails on the types of queries enterprise engineers actually ask:

Standard RAG
Retrieves text, hopes LLM figures it out
Finds documents mentioning an entity. Cannot traverse relationships, check constraints, compare versions, or resolve entity types. No structured precision — everything is fuzzy matching.
Knowledge Fabric
Understands structure, traverses relationships
Knows what an entity is, what depends on it, what conflicts with it, and what changed about it. Combines graph precision with semantic coverage. Every answer is cited.
The Difference in Practice

Standard RAG: "Find documents mentioning Feature X" → returns 20 loosely relevant chunks.
Knowledge Fabric: "What depends on Feature X, what conflicts with it, what parameters does it control, and what's the recommended configuration for Scenario Y?" → returns a structured, cited, traversal-backed answer in one round.

Data Ingestion: Keeping the Fabric Fresh

A Knowledge Fabric is only as good as its data currency. The ingestion pipeline transforms raw documents into the multi-layer representation automatically — no manual curation required.

  • Document Acquisition
    Automated detection and download of new or updated documents from source repositories. Multiple formats: PDF, HTML, JSON, XML, Excel.
  • Parsing & Extraction
    Domain-specific parsers extract structured content — tables, parameters, entities, relationships, metrics, and cross-references from each document type.
  • Entity Resolution & Registration
    Every extracted entity is resolved against the entity registry. New entities are registered with their type. Duplicates and aliases are merged.
  • Graph Construction
    Relationships between entities are materialized as graph edges — dependencies, conflicts, containment, parameter ownership, metric mapping.
  • Embedding & Indexing
    Text content is chunked, enriched with entity metadata, embedded, and indexed in the vector store with hybrid retrieval configuration.
  • Cross-Link Materialization
    Bridge layer indices are rebuilt — connecting entities across domain boundaries for multi-hop traversal.

The AI Agent: One Round, All Parallel

The Knowledge Fabric is accessed through a tool-equipped AI agent that orchestrates retrieval across layers. The agent's design follows a strict set of principles:

Routing
Entity-First Routing
Every query starts with entity resolution. The agent identifies what the user is asking about before deciding how to retrieve information. This prevents wasted tool calls and ensures precision.
Execution
Parallel Tool Execution
The agent calls all required tools in a single parallel block. It never chains sequential calls where parallel execution is possible. This minimizes latency and maximizes throughput.
Integrity
Citation-Mandatory Output
Every factual claim in the response must trace to a specific tool result. Claims without citations are treated as hallucinations and removed. The agent renders tool results — it never invents.
Priority
Structured Over Semantic
When structured data (typed facts, graph relationships) is available, it takes precedence over semantic retrieval. Semantic search fills gaps — it doesn't override precision.

Multiple Access Patterns

The Knowledge Fabric is consumed through multiple interfaces, each suited to different workflows:

IDE
MCP Protocol — IDE Integration
Model Context Protocol server exposes the fabric's tools directly inside coding assistants (Claude Code, Copilot). Engineers query documentation without leaving their development environment.
Visual
Interactive Dashboard
Visual exploration interface with chat, graph visualization, dependency viewers, timeline comparisons, and scenario planners. For deep investigation and planning workflows.
Programmatic
REST API
Programmatic access for CI/CD integration, automated validation, and batch queries. Enables fabric-powered checks in deployment pipelines.
Reasoning
Conversational Agent
Full reasoning agent for complex multi-step queries that require planning, traversal across multiple layers, and synthesized answers from diverse sources.

Design Principles

Principle
Entity-First Resolution
Every query resolves "what is this?" before "what about it?" The entity registry provides sub-100ms type resolution, enabling the system to skip irrelevant layers entirely and route to the correct retrieval path.
Principle
Graph + Semantic Fusion
Structured graph for precision (conflicts, dependencies, constraints). Semantic search for coverage (fuzzy matching, cross-document discovery, procedural knowledge). Neither alone is sufficient.
Principle
Zero Hallucination by Design
Every claim traces to a source. No citation = assertion deleted. The agent is instructed to render tool results, not synthesize from parametric memory. Structured data always overrides semantic guesses.
Principle
Always Fresh
Automated pipelines detect new documents, parse them, extract entities and relationships, update the graph, and re-index — keeping the fabric current without manual intervention.

Performance Characteristics

<100ms
Entity Resolution
1 Round
Agent Execution
100%
Cited Answers
N Layers
Parallel Retrieval
Multi-Hop
Cross-Domain
"The Knowledge Fabric doesn't replace documentation — it makes documentation queryable, connected, and alive. Every answer traces back to a source. Every relationship is computable. Every conflict is detectable before it reaches production."
— The shift from document retrieval to knowledge intelligence
entry.summary: Transform scattered technical documentation into an AI-queryable intelligence layer — connecting features, parameters, dependencies, and metrics into a unified graph.
